articles.title: Jeff Bezos says people have been ‘incorrectly’ taught that success is a villain: ‘You can be a billionaire if you started a hamburger stand’
articles.summary: With $372 billion to his name, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says Americans have been taught to view billionaire success in the wrong light.
articles.body:
Jeff Bezos has taken Amazon from an online bookstore he founded in his garage in 1994—to the No. 1 company on the Fortune 500 . His own net worth has soared, too, reaching $372 billion and making him the second-richest person in the world.

However, the 62-year-old argues that people who view extreme wealth like his own as a bad thing have been taught to think about success the wrong way.

"I think we live in an environment where some people have been taught, I think incorrectly, but taught … this whole kind of oppressor/oppressed framework, and [that] success is villainy," Bezos recently told Fox News .

"Success is not villainy. You can be a billionaire if you started a hamburger stand."

Bezos pointed to how someone could start with a simple food stand with 10 or so workers, grow it into a business with thousands of locations and employees, and eventually become a billionaire.

"This is how it works," he said. "There's nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love. And it doesn't make him a bad person."

As Americans question billionaire wealth, Jeff Bezos argues for tackling affordability

Many people, particularly younger generations, may disagree with Bezos's assessment. Some 18% of Americans view being extremely rich as "morally wrong," a figure that nearly doubles to about 33% among Gen Z adults ages 18 to 29, according to a 2025 Pew Research study .

That skepticism comes as billionaire wealth continues to soar. In 2025, the fortunes of the world's billionaires reached a record $18.3 trillion, according to Oxfam . Meanwhile, the American Dream of buying a home has increasingly felt out of reach for many households, particularly younger Americans struggling with housing costs.

Bezos, for his part, acknowledged that the country races real affordability problems . But he argued that voters should be wary of politicians who focus on assigning blame rather than addressing the underlying problems.

"You can't pretend there's no problems," he said. "Young people look at the cost of housing and think, 'I have to live two hours out of town. I can't live close to my job.'"

It's the same problem-solving approach he expects from executives at his own companies.

"If there's somebody at Amazon or Blue Origin or Prometheus, an executive at one of my companies, instead of working on a root cause and a real fix, all they did is point fingers and blame people, we would exit them quickly," Bezos said. "They wouldn't be here long."

Earlier this year, Bezos floated a proposal to ease the tax burden on lower-income Americans, suggesting that the bottom half of U.S. income earners—roughly 76 million households—should pay no federal income taxes.

"The bottom half of income earners in this country pay only 3% of the taxes," Bezos told CNBC in May. "I think it should be zero."

The billionaire pointed to a hypothetical health care worker in Queens who makes $75,000 a year—but pays more than $1,000 a month in taxes.

"To me, it's kind of absurd that we're doing this," Bezos said. "We shouldn't be asking this nurse in Queens to send money to Washington. They should be sending her an apology. It really makes no sense."

From Howard Schultz to Jamie Dimon, billionaire CEOs agree with Bezos that success shouldn't be vilified

Bezos isn't alone in pushing back against the idea that success—and the billions of dollars that can come with it—should be viewed as inherently bad.

Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz , who has about $3.4 billion to his name, has also argued that his fortune reflects years of hard work rather than an unfair advantage.

"This moniker 'billionaire,' let's get at that okay?" Schultz said during a heated U.S. Senate committee hearing in 2023. "I grew up in federally subsidized housing; my parents never owned a home; I came from nothing. I thought my entire life was based on the achievement of the American Dream. Yes, I have billions of dollars. I earned it. No one gave it to me."

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has a net worth of about $3 billion, has similarly acknowledged concerns about wealth inequality while pushing back against the idea that wealthy people should be vilified simply for their success.

Dimon told 60 Minutes in 2019: "I think you should vilify Nazis, but you shouldn't vilify people who've worked hard to accomplish things."

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: ATF suspends federal registration and approval rules for certain firearms
articles.summary: The ATF announced it will no longer require federal registration for silencers, short-barreled rifles and shotguns after Congress zeroed out NFA taxes.
articles.body: Gun owners will no longer be required to federally register or seek advance approval to manufacture or transfer silencers, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and "Any Other Weapons" (AOWs), the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) announced Friday. The policy directive halts National Firearms Act (NFA) enforcement for items subject to zero-dollar tax rates under the updated guidelines. In a letter to federal firearms licensees, ATF Director Robert Cekada noted that the move follows a federal court decision invalidating key manufacturing and transfer provisions of the NFA. GUN RIGHTS GETS 'GREATEST RESTORATION' IN 100 YEARS WITH LATEST TRUMP DOJ MOVE, LAWMAKER HAILS "The direction from the President, Congress, and the courts is clear," Cekada said. "ATF is now following suit with our enforcement posture while continuing to ensure we remain focused where we are needed the most: combatting violent crime in American communities." The regulatory shift stems from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in which Congress reduced NFA manufacturing and transfer taxes to $0 for silencers, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, and AOWs. GUN RIGHTS GROUPS CAPITALIZE AFTER JUDGE REVERSES DECADES-OLD RESTRICTIONS: 'MONUMENTAL' Following that legislation, a federal judge in Texas issued an injunction in August, concluding that because Congress eliminated the underlying tax, the NFA’s mandatory registration and transfer provisions could no longer be justified under Congress’s constitutional taxing power. The ruling initially applied only to the plaintiffs, but the Justice Department subsequently extended its nonenforcement policy nationwide. John Commerford, executive director of the National Rifle Association (NRA), praised the announcement, calling it a historic milestone. MAJOR APPEALS COURT DECLARES NEW JERSEY AR-15 BAN UNCONSTITUTIONAL IN LANDMARK SECOND AMENDMENT RULING "This is what happens when all three branches of government are willing to follow the Constitution," Commerford said in a statement. "Now the Trump administration has confirmed it will stop treating law-abiding Americans as if they still need special permission from the government to own hearing protection, rifles, or shotguns." Although the specific NFA requirements and fees have been suspended, all transactions remain subject to the Gun Control Act. Licensed dealers are still required to perform standard background checks and maintain transaction records. Machine guns and destructive devices remain subject to NFA requirements, while federal approval is still required to transport short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns across state lines. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The ATF noted it will continue to accept voluntary registrations for owners wishing to document their items, though future legal shifts could potentially reinstate prior regulations without automatic grandfathering protection.

articles.title: Mamdani unveils sweeping NYPD use-of-force review, but stops short of fulfilling key campaign promises
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani launched a New York Police Department use-of-force review after the Win Rozario shooting, but it falls short of campaign pledges.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the launch of an internal review of the New York Police Department’s use of force on Monday, but the initiative falls short of fulfilling several of his campaign promises, including pledges to disband a controversial police unit and eliminate a database of suspected gang members. "When the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest," Mamdani said in a press release. "Every New Yorker deserves to know that force will be used lawfully, carefully and only when necessary." More than nine months after taking office, Mamdani has yet to fulfill several campaign pledges, including disbanding the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, eliminating its database of suspected gang members and shifting police resources away from low-level offenses. NYPD COP FOUND GUILTY OF CHOKEHOLD IN FIRST CONVICTION SINCE RESTRAINT TACTIC BANNED AFTER GEORGE FLOYD DEATH The review comes after the May 2026 retirement of one of the officers involved in the 2024 shooting of 19-year-old Win Rozario — a development that came before any disciplinary trial could take place. Video footage of the confrontation, captured in March 2024, shows officers responding to a house call, placed by Rozario himself. An altercation ensued when Rozario, who was experiencing a mental health crisis, reacted adversely to the police presence, prompting the police to use Tasers on him. Unsubdued, Rozario then grabbed a pair of scissors and advanced on officers, who shot him at close range. New York Attorney General Letitia James' office declined to bring criminal charges against the officers in December 2025, concluding that prosecutors could not disprove beyond a reasonable doubt that their use of deadly force was justified under state law. The mayor framed his initiative as a way to strengthen and improve accountability. Mamdani’s initiative comes with an additional $2.6 million in funding for the Office of Inspector General for the NYPD. Additionally, the NYPD will also notify state authorities when officers facing disciplinary charges retire, allowing the state to consider decertification and helping prevent those officers from avoiding scrutiny by joining another law enforcement agency. Those changes will accompany a use-of-force review which, according to Mamdani, is the first of its kind in over a decade and will include a "robust community engagement process." "We have an obligation to Win’s family and to every New Yorker who calls for help in a moment of crisis. This review is about making sure our policies reflect that responsibility," Mamdani said. MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS MAMDANI WALKS BACK PLAN TO INCREASE NYPD HEADCOUNT FOLLOWING DSA PRESSURE Notably, the proposed adjustments fall short of campaign promises that Mamdani made to eliminate certain policing activity. In particular, Mamdani called for an end to NYPD arrests on charges of lower–level crimes like public urination and open container violations, noting that such activity was making it harder for officers to tackle violent crimes. "The fact that every year we ask them to take on additional responsibilities – we are making it more and more difficult for them to respond to the very responsibilities that drew them to the job in the first place," Mamdani said last fall. During his tenure, public urination summonses have gone up, climbing 18%, according to recent reporting. Mamdani also promised to end a database of suspected gang members. He also demanded an end to the Strategic Response Group (SRG), a policing task force that had received public attention for aggressive tactics in subduing protests. "As Mayor, I will disband the SRG, which has cost taxpayers millions in lawsuit settlements + brutalized countless New Yorkers exercising their First Amendment rights," Mamdani said in a post to X shortly after announcing his bid for mayor. LETITIA JAMES’ TIMES SQUARE SHOOTING PROBE DRAWS GOP CRITICISM OVER NEW YORK’S MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS In addition to keeping those elements in place, Mamdani also retained Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, who was appointed by Mamdani’s predecessor, Eric Adams. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether his police reform plans have taken a different path than the one he originally outlined before taking office.

articles.title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.summary: While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little.
articles.body:
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.

Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.

"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.

"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."

Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.

It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.

"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.

"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.

"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.

"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.

"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."

In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.

In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.

Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.

Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel .

Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.

Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.

Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.

It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.

"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.

"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.

On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.

That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.

Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.

Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.

On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.

"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.

The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.

Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

As buzz around potential 2028 presidential candidates grows, a new poll shows clear frontrunners in hypothetical Democratic and Republican primaries.

In a new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released Sunday, Oct. 11, it was a battle of the VPs: Former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance both led their respective party's potential primary.

According to the survey, Harris leads among Democrats with 30% support, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 15% and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg tied at 9%.

On the other side of the aisle, Vance leads with 38% of Republicans, followed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 24%, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis receiving 9% of support from GOP respondents.

The poll surveyed 2,553 U.S. adults from Oct. 2 to Oct. 5, according to Focaldata .

articles.title: Cooper leads Whatley by at least 7 points in new NC Senate polls
articles.summary: New polling released Monday showed North Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by at least 7 points, weeks ahead of the November midterm elections. The Trafalgar Group’s polling showed Cooper’s lead at 48.8 percent, with Whatley behind at 40.9 percent. Polling also showed Cooper with larger support among different age demographics,…
articles.body:
New polling released Monday showed North Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by at least 7 points, weeks ahead of the November midterm elections.

The Trafalgar Group’s polling showed Cooper’s lead at 48.8 percent, with Whatley behind at 40.9 percent. Polling also showed Cooper with larger support among different age demographics, with younger voters between aged 18-29 backing him at 69 percent, along with voters aged 30-39 at 68.4 percent.

Voters 65 and older favored him less than Whatley, with 50.2 percent choosing Whatley over the 39.9 percent backing Cooper.

Cooper also led among the 20.5 percent of Black respondents to the poll, receiving 67.1 percent support compared to 20.8 percent for Whatley.

These results resemble similar statistics from an East Carolina University’s Center for Survey Research poll released Thursday that found Cooper led Whatley by 7 points, at 50-43, with 6 percent saying they were undecided.

Aggregate polling from The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) showed Cooper with a 48.9 percent probability of winning if the election had been held that day, with Whatley having a 40.5 percent probability.

Both candidates seek to succeed retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Democrats’ stakes in the Senate are high as they look for any opportunity to flip GOP-held seats to regain their majority, needing at least four seats and losing none.

Chris Cooper, a professor of public policy at Western Carolina University, previously told The Hill that the state’s demographics are not becoming bluer but that there is a balance in the rural parts of the state. North Carolina has a Democratic governor in Josh Stein, some Democratic state officials and a Republican majority in the state House.

Chris Cooper, no relation to the Senate candidate, said Democrats are also benefiting from Whatley’s status as being relatively unknown in the state compared with the four-time attorney general and two-term governor.

Whatley served as the Republican National Committee chair from 2024-25, playing a role in Trump’s second reelection contest. He previously served as North Carolina’s Republican Party chair.

The Trafalgar survey was conducted Oct. 8-10 and included 1,091 respondents. The margin of error is 2.9 percentage points.

articles.body:
Synthetically concentrated kratom derivatives draw federal attention

The spread of “gas station opioid” products derived from the kratom plant is causing concern for federal authorities and lawmakers.

© Alejandra Villa Loarca/Newsday RM via Getty Images

The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) signaled heightened concerns about kratom-derived extracts earlier this year when it announced plans to temporarily ban products containing concentrations of 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) , mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) , MGM-15 and MGM-16 .

The agency is aiming to temporarily classify these substances as Schedule I under the Controlled Substances Act. This action would not affect the natural herbal form of kratom also sold over the counter.

Kratom’s legal status varies from state to state. Nine states have fully banned the herb while more than 30 states regulate the sale of it on some level with have caps on 7-OH concentrations. In more than a dozen other states, kratom exists in a legal gray area, neither banned nor strictly regulated.

Since around 2010, products containing synthetically concentrated extracts like 7-OH and other related compounds, that occur in just trace amounts in the plant, have become readily available over the counter at gas stations and tobacco shops.

Oliver Grundmann, clinical professor in the Department of Medicinal Chemistry at the University of Florida, told The Hill that scheduling these highly concentrated products is warranted given that Schedule I classification indicates a drug has no accepted medical use.

Determining a medical use would require going through the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) approval process.

“That is clearly not what any of these manufacturers that sell [7-OH] products want to do, and therefore it is adequate at the moment, given what we know about [7-OH], to place it into controlled substances schedule,” Grundmann said.

articles.title: Trump says Kimberly Guilfoyle could be fired as Greece envoy after alleged misconduct
articles.summary: "We're not happy," says the president about his son's ex-fiancée following reports of improper behaviour.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is weighing firing the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of her alleged improper behaviour in Athens, which she has denied.

Asked if he was considering sacking her, Trump told reporters at the White House: "We're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy." She is the ex-fiancée of the president's son, Donald Trump Jr.

The Wall Street Journal reported Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration.

Her lawyers denied any wrongdoing by Guilfoyle and said she was owed the money for speaking engagements and consulting work for the donor.

Guilfoyle, 57, a former Fox News host and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was appointed as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.

At the time, Trump said "her extensive experience and leadership in law, media and politics, along with her sharp intellect make her supremely qualified" to represent the US abroad.

A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by the Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.

In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."

Deters never sent the money. Guilfoyle's lawyers have disputed the authenticity of the messages.

They said in a two-page statement on 12 October that Deters owed Guilfoyle about $150,000 for speeches and consulting work that she performed for him long before her ambassadorship.

"Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption," they said.

Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle boasting of her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.

According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.

Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees have been calling on the state department to investigate her conduct in Greece.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured with Guilfoyle last week during his trip to Athens, was also reported to be unhappy with her in light of the allegations.

A former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, she joined Fox News in 2006.

After leaving broadcasting in 2018, she joined the Trump campaign. The same year, she began a relationship with Donald Jr, and the couple eventually became engaged.

The pair reportedly parted ways in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.

Donald Jr wed socialite and model Bettina Anderson last year in Florida.

articles.title: Spicer says he’s ‘absolutely’ concerned about Kansas Senate race
articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Sean Spicer on Monday said he is “absolutely” concerned about Republicans losing the Kansas Senate race, which election handicappers say could flip in favor of the Democrats. NewsNation’s “The Hill” host Blake Burman asked Spicer if he had any worry that Republicans could lose the Kansas Senate seat helmed by…
articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Sean Spicer on Monday said he is “absolutely” concerned about Republicans losing the Kansas Senate race, which election handicappers say could flip in favor of the Democrats.

NewsNation’s “The Hill” host Blake Burman asked Spicer if he had any worry that Republicans could lose the Kansas Senate seat helmed by Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.), with Democrat Adam Hamilton eyeing to win his seat.

“Absolutely. Absolutely,” Spicer replied. “In fact, when I had Tim Scott, the senator from South Carolina, who’s chairman of the Republican Senatorial Committee, on my show on Friday, I ended the interview very Blake Berman-esque.”

“And I said, ‘Senator, if Trump calls you and says, I can only go to three states, what are they?'” Spicer continued. “And he mentioned Alaska, where Trump was already going. And then he said Kansas. And I said, ‘Really?’ And I think he realized when he admitted that Kansas would be on that list, what that meant, and there’s no question Kansas on the list.”

Spicer added that he predicts Kansas, Alaska and Iowa “will all come home” for Republicans. He then predicted that the GOP could lose five to seven seats in the House.

“Again, 22 days out, if we can get our numbers to perform better, get some of these low-propensity voters that are Trump supporters that don’t generally vote in midterms, and we’ve had this problem the last three midterms,” he said. “If we can do something to turn them out and make the case as to why what the Democrats are doing is utterly extreme, and we’ll take this country in a very different direction, I think that we can pull this over the finish line.”

The Cook Political Report shows the race between Marshall and Hamilton as a toss-up. But it still gives Marshall the advantage by 8 points.

The election handicapper cited Hamilton’s performance in the race as being more of a moderate voice and that support gained by President Trump has eroded due to struggles with agriculture over rising fuel and fertilizer costs, which have soared in the months after the Iran war began.

Hamilton has also received several high-profile endorsements , including from former Kansas Govs. Mike Hayden (R) and Bill Graves (R).

But he has also received scrutiny over his handling of a child sexual abuse scandal at his church. Meanwhile, Marshall has faced pushback scrutiny over his handling of taxpayer funds and for suing hundreds of patients over medical debt.

Aggregate polling from The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ shows Marshall with a 65 percent probability of winning compared to the 35 percent probability for Hamilton.

Were Hamilton to win, he would be the first Democrat elected by Kansans to the Senate since former Sen. George McGill (D-Kan.) in 1932.

articles.title: Trump attacks Rep. Ilhan Omar and Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at Ohio rally
articles.summary: The crowd chanted “deport” at several points as Trump denigrated Omar, who was born in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S., and El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan.
articles.body: Chants of “deport” rang out Monday night as President Donald Trump criticized Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, at a rally for Republican candidates in Youngstown, Ohio. “I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said of Omar, whose home in Washington, D.C., was searched hours earlier by federal agents, two people familiar with the investigation told NBC News. A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” as “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The statement did not specify that the investigation was related to Omar, nor did it provide more information about the search. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” Trump then spoke of Somali gang activity in Minnesota and what the FBI has described as a recently thwarted shooting at the state’s Mall of America, alleged to have been plotted by an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, The Associated Press reported. That’s when the first wave of “deport” chants began. Omar, who was born in the war-torn country of Somalia, immigrated to the U.S. as a child decades ago. El-Sayed was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar wrote earlier Monday on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Trump said he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home. At the rally, he segued from his attack on Omar and people of Somali descent in Minnesota to an attack on El-Sayed. “These people are crazy,” Trump said. “You look at the guy running in Michigan. He’s a jihadist.” Trump went on to praise El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, before he again referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and proclaimed that “Somalia bandits, Third World gangsters, jihadist sympathizers do not belong in Ohio.” He added: “They don’t belong in America. Better get them the hell out of here.” More chants of “deport” then erupted from the audience at Youngstown’s Covelli Centre. A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night. Last week, after Trump referred to him on social media by his middle name, Mohamed, El-Sayed condemned it as a tactic meant to raise fears about his religion. “They point to my name and they point to my faith, trying to distract us from the challenges that we have,” El-Sayed, who is Muslim, told supporters at an event Thursday in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “My name did not raise your gas prices. My faith is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” Trump’s remarks Monday continued his leading role in ratcheting up rhetoric around Muslims and immigrants. Days after El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Trump warned that the U.S. could become a “jihadist-run country.” And Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., accused El-Sayed of sympathizing with Osama bin Laden as he was campaigning with Rogers last week in Michigan. Trump was in Ohio’s Mahoning Valley — a once reliably Democratic region that has become increasingly Republican since his rise in politics — to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the state’s GOP nominee for governor. It was his second visit to Ohio in less than 10 days. His last trip, to the Dayton area, included remarks about nearby Springfield. During a 2024 presidential debate, Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets. Trump mentioned Springfield again Monday in Youngstown, immediately after his attacks on Omar and El-Sayed. “All of a sudden, they dropped 35,000 people in from Haiti, and it didn’t work out too well,” he said before he defiantly repeated his past falsehoods. “Remember during the debate I said some of the things they were doing? I was right.”

articles.body:
President Trump repeatedly brought up Minnesota and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday night while stumping for Republicans in Ohio ahead of the midterms.

Federal agents searched the home of Omar, a Somali-born American citizen, on Monday as part of a federal criminal investigation into Omar.

“Just look at what’s happening in the once great state of Minnesota. What a mess they have done,” Trump said in Youngstown. “And Ilhan, somebody was asking. I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: she’s a disaster.”

He said Omar comes from “one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

The crowd started chanting “deport” as he talked about Somalis in the U.S.

He brought up the massive pandemic-era fraud scheme that took place in Minnesota and involved some of the state’s Somali community. Hundreds of millions of dollars were stolen from a federally funded nutrition program.

“They came over here. They had nothing. They came from a government that doesn’t exist,” the president said. “They come from a part of the world that only knows how to kill each other.”

He accused Democrats in Minnesota of cheating in the elections, saying he thought he won the state in 2024 before “a rather large drop of votes” showed up. Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris won Minnesota in 2024.

“They cheat like hell. Aside from everything else, they cheat on the elections,” he said.

Earlier Monday Trump called Omar “ totally crooked ” after being asked about the federal agents searching her home.

“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Ohio. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” he continued. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Last week, Trump said Minnesotans should “fight back” against the Somali immigrants in their state.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”

Minnesota has the largest population of Somalis in the U.S. and 1.07 percent, according to World Population Review . Most arrived as refugees, like Omar and her family, after a civil war in the country in the 90s.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday slammed the federal search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) Washington, D.C., home, saying that her citizenship “should not be weaponized” against her.

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — the investigative arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — carried out the search, a Justice Department (DOJ) spokesperson told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. The DOJ said it was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

Mamdani lambasted what he said was the federal government using “the full force of the Department of Homeland Security against a sitting member of Congress for the offense of disagreeing with the White House.”

“The path to citizenship should not be weaponized against anyone, including Rep. Ilhan Omar, a naturalized American who swore an oath to this country — the same one that I took,” Mamdani wrote on the social platform X . “The promise of citizenship should not be contingent on someone agreeing with the federal government.”

Mamdani, who himself became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2018 , referred to Omar’s citizenship status. The member of the progressive House crew “The Squad” entered the U.S. after her family sought asylum from Somalia amid its civil war. Omar received her citizenship in 2000.

She said she was “ok” following the raid, but she called the incident “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she wrote on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

President Trump on Monday told reporters outside the White House that investigators are looking into Omar “very carefully.”

“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it.”

DOJ does not typically take major actions against candidates for office in the 60 days preceding an election. The midterm elections are in three weeks.

Lawmakers and Trump critics slammed the raid , with House Democratic leadership in a joint statement calling it “deeply disturbing” and that it raised questions about the weaponization of government.

“Squad” member Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) likened the search to fascism.

“DHS raiding a member of Congress’s home is exactly what a fascist police state does,” she wrote on X . “This president should not be able to weaponize the federal government against political enemies. I stand with Ilhan.”

Omar entered Congress in 2018, among a wave of new Democratic lawmakers ushered in during Trump’s first term. She has been a longtime critic of the president, and he has levied numerous allegations against the congresswoman over her immigration status, accusing the Somali native of fraudulently obtaining U.S. citizenship. Omar denies this claim.

The administration announced it was investigating Omar last year for alleged immigration fraud after Trump and others claimed without evidence that Omar married her brother in order to obtain U.S. citizenship.

Tensions between the two escalated after Trump attacked Minnesota’s Somali refugee community in connection with the state’s fraud scandal earlier this year.

articles.title: Sanders calls for artificial superintelligence ban after OpenAI CEO interview

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Monday called for permanently banning artificial superintelligence in response to recent remarks made by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Altman told Politico’s “Decoded” podcast in an interview last week that society will face a “coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” coming from open-source AI models. He also said that people will “have to just accept some fairly severe cyber incidents from open models, in exchange for the liberty that comes with that.”

“No, Mr. Altman. We won’t accept a severe AI cyberattack in exchange for ‘liberty,'” Sanders wrote on the social platform X , later asking, “Mr. Altman: What do you mean by that?”

Sanders wrote that Americans “are not willing to accept disaster ‘in exchange for the liberty’ of making Big Tech Oligarchs even richer and more powerful,” adding that tech developers working on AI “are not above the law.”

“If you and other Big Tech Oligarchs make products that commit crimes or disasters, we will hold you accountable for breaking the law — no matter how much wealth and power you have,” Sanders continued. “We must PAUSE advanced AI and permanently BAN artificial superintelligence before it is too late.”

Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) last month introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act which would institute the permanent ban, along with temporarily pausing “advanced AI development” until federal regulators establish safety standards.

The bill would also direct the U.S. to seek diplomatic agreements to prevent the development of superintelligence and establish a Cabinet-level federal agency to focus on AI safety rules.

This bill is the latest of several proposals floated by progressives in Congress to slow down AI development amid recent cybersecurity incidents and hacks involving rogue AI software, including an unsuccessful hack of the Department of Education’s website and a hack of Australia’s health department .

The chorus of concern grew after former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned last month that AI could pose an existential threat to human life on Earth.

Sanders, who sided with Pope Leo XIV’s warnings about AI’s impact on the art world , slammed President Trump over his response to developing AI.

“Look, it is embarrassing, really, I think, going beyond politics, how ignorant this president is about the dangers of AI,” Sanders told MS NOW last month .

Trump said he would launch an “ AI czar ” and has launched a “ Super Intelligence Force ” in response to the technology’s development, but has praised AI’s possibilities despite the bipartisan calls for regulation.

The president has sought to rebrand AI as “ super intelligence , and recently signed a pledge with tech executives that put the name in writing across the executive branch.

articles.title: Florida Republican running for re-election snags presidential endorsement — from Colombia
articles.summary: Rep. María Elvira Salazar has received political support from right-wing stalwarts overseas as she finds herself on the outs with President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who faces a tightening race in her heavily Hispanic congressional district, picked up a presidential endorsement Monday — but not from the Oval Office occupant. Colombia’s president, the Trump-allied Abelardo de la Espriella, called Salazar “Colombia’s best friend in U.S. Congress” in a Spanish-language video Salazar posted on X. De la Espriella, a Colombian-American citizen who owns property in Salazar’s district, and his wife have donated nearly $90,000 to Salazar in the past. Salazar made waves last month when she broke with President Donald Trump over immigration, directly addressing him in an ad in which she said some of his immigration enforcement efforts had gone “too far.” “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said. She is one of several Republicans to have distanced themselves from Trump as the midterm elections approach. In the days after the ad aired, Trump told reporters at the White House that “without me she wouldn’t have gotten elected,” adding that Salazar “got a little bit soft on the border” while saying he still supported her campaign. Trump later attacked Salazar, using Truth Social posts to boost other users’ messages attacking her — including one calling for a new Republican to replace her, even though the election is only weeks away. Now, on the outs with Trump, Salazar is getting support from some right-wing stalwarts overseas. Last week, she posted a video endorsement from Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who called her a “firm and loyal ally to the cause of Venezuelan freedom.” Salazar is seeking re-election in a district where more than 74% of the population is Hispanic, according to census data. A significant part of the district has ties to Colombia and Venezuela. Salazar has represented the district since 2021. It has swung dramatically among presidential candidates in recent elections. Trump won the district by 15 percentage points in 2024, while former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won it by 20 points in 2016. According to an NBC News poll, Latino voters nationwide are souring on Trump, dissatisfied over high prices and his approach to immigration enforcement. Salazar is seeking to fend off Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, a former CBS News Miami anchor. The race, not originally expected to be competitive, has picked up steam in recent weeks. Cook Political Report shifted the race toward Democrats in late September, moving it from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican.” The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, meanwhile, said last week that it was sending additional resources to the district in hope of flipping the seat, adding it to its “Red to Blue” program. Reached for comment about the Latin American leaders’ endorsements of his opponent, Rodriguez turned the conversation to domestic issues, saying the district’s families are “struggling with skyrocketing housing, insurance, grocery and healthcare costs.” “As much as my opponent would like to make this election about politics in Latin America, it’s really about the people of Florida’s 27th District,” Rodriguez said. “Those are the people I answer to, those are the problems I intend to solve, and those are the people I will represent in Congress.” De la Espriella, who calls himself “the Tiger,” emerged as a flag-bearer of the Latin American right after his election in June. He got a boost after he received Trump’s endorsement shortly before his runoff against leftist Colombian Sen. Iván Cepeda, an ally of former Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who often found himself in Trump’s crosshairs. The channel between de la Espriella and Congress goes both ways. Several lawmakers, including Salazar and Colombian-born Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who advises Trump on Latin American policy, endorsed de la Espriella before his election this year.

articles.title: Newsom backs California ballot measure that cancels out billionaire tax proposal
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) endorsed a ballot measure that, if approved by voters, would cancel out the ballot measure proposal that would impose a one-time tax on the Golden State’s billionaires. On Friday, Newsom endorsed Proposition 42, which would prohibit retroactive taxes imposed by Proposition 40, known as the Billionaire Tax Act, for any…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) endorsed a ballot measure that, if approved by voters, would cancel out the ballot measure proposal that would impose a one-time tax on the Golden State’s billionaires.

On Friday, Newsom endorsed Proposition 42, which would prohibit retroactive taxes imposed by Proposition 40, known as the Billionaire Tax Act, for any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026, CalMatters reported .

Proposition 42 was funded by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin as a means to defeat the billionaire tax, the outlet reported. It would also ban any new taxes on personal property, including pensions and 401K accounts before retirees collect income from them, along with other investments.

“We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents of the measure, obtained by CalMatters.

The Billionaire Tax Act would impose a 5 percent tax and allocate 90 percent of the collected tax revenue for healthcare programs and 10 percent for food assistance or education-related programs.

Newsom has long been a vocal opponent of Proposition 50, writing on Substack in June that it is not how California should set its budget priorities. He urged that the U.S. –– not California –– pass a billionaire tax.

“I will continue to oppose the November measure because I believe California’s budget belongs to all Californians, not to any one stakeholder, no matter how worthy the cause,” he wrote. “And I will keep making the case, here and everywhere I can, that the fight against concentrated wealth is a national fight that we have to win soon.”

Proposition 50 qualified for the November ballot in June, exceeding the 962,106 valid signatures expected to back the initiative.

The ballot initiative has divided some California Democrats who argue it could push billionaires out of the state — particularly in Silicon Valley. Brin previously warned that the tax will undermine California businesses and force business leaders out of state.

But the measure has received support from the Service Employees International Union United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), one of the measure’s most prominent backers, as well as progressive lawmakers like Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who rallied support for the measure in Los Angeles earlier this year.

Proposition 40 saw growing support earlier in the year, but last month’s University of California, Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll showed that it has a narrow lead from backers. Forty-five percent of registered California voters support the measure, while 43 percent said they oppose it, with 12 percent of respondents saying they are undecided.

articles.title: Protester punched in face by Trump supporter, mocked by president at Ohio rally: 'Gotta go on a diet'
articles.summary: A supporter of President Donald Trump punched a heckler wearing a "Release the Epstein Files" shirt at the president's Youngstown, Ohio, rally.
articles.body: A heckler wearing a "Release the Epstein Files" shirt was punched in the face by an apparent supporter of President Donald Trump during a rally Monday in Youngstown, Ohio, before the president mocked the protester's weight. Trump was criticizing Ohio Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted after losing his Senate seat in 2024, when rally attendees shifted their attention toward a confrontation in the crowd. Video of the confrontation showed a rallygoer who appeared to support Trump shoving the heckler and striking her in the face as the crowd chanted "USA!" TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS The man also grabbed the woman by the hair and attempted to slam her face toward the ground. Police eventually intervened and broke up the fight before escorting the woman out of the venue. Video showed the man who struck her remaining in the arena and exchanging high-fives with other attendees. Trump appeared to notice the disruption and accused the protester of being paid to interrupt the rally, although he offered no evidence to support the allegation. He also mocked the protester's weight. ANTI-TRUMP PROTESTER CHARGED AFTER VIRAL VIDEO APPEARS TO SHOW JOURNALIST SHOVED AT MAINE PROTEST "He's a paid protester," Trump said, appearing to be unaware that the heckler was a woman. "They’re all paid. They get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They’re scum. But he’s going back home to Mom. He’s going back home to Mom. Look at him. Look at him. Terrible. Don’t we love law enforcement? Oh, he’s gotta go on a diet! He’s a fat guy. Wow. Wow. Gotta go on a diet fast. We all do." "No, they’re paid protesters. That’s a very low-class protester," the president added. The woman's "Release the Epstein Files" shirt comes as Trump and his Justice Department face bipartisan scrutiny over the delay in the release of additional documents related to the investigations into deceased sex predator Jeffrey Epstein. articles.title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
articles.summary: An in-depth look at the key polling, races and issues ahead of an election that will define Trump’s final two years as president.
articles.body:
Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.

Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.

Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.

One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.

He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.

The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.

Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.

But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.

The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.

Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.

The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.

Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.

Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.

Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.

The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US.

The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.

Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.

Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.

Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.

Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.

One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.

At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m).

On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.

The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.

More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact . Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.

Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.

Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.

articles.title: Muere el padre del expresidente Zapatero, a los 100 años
articles.standfirst: Juan Rodríguez, progenitor del expolítico socialista, que fue jurista
articles.summary: Juan Rodríguez, progenitor del expolítico socialista, que fue jurista
articles.body: Golpe anímico para el expresidente del Gobierno José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero. Su padre, Juan Rodríguez, ha muerto a la edad de 100 años en León, que es de donde procedía la familia. El fallecido, que era jurista de formación, fue hijo de un represaliado en 1936 por mantenerse fiel a la II República, el capitán de infantería Juan Rodríguez Lozano. Han sido fuentes del PSOE las que han informado de su defunción en la tarde de este lunes, día de la Hispanidad y de las Fuerzas Armadas. La base de la familia Rodríguez Zapatero se ha cimentado por su presencia en León. Formó parte del ámbito político y jurídico de la ciudad castellano-leonesa, donde la familia mantiene desde hace décadas una influencia significativa. Se licenció en Derecho y ejerció como abogado del Ayuntamiento de León en los servicios jurídicos consistoriales. Fue una figura muy influyente en el expresidente del Gobierno por el PSOE entre 2004 y 2011. Juan quedó viudo de su esposa Purificación Zapatero en el año 2000 y los últimos años estaba ingresado en una residencia. “Tenía muchísima ascendencia sobre la abogacía en León, tenía uno de los despachos más importantes y de los pocos progresistas, era muy querido en la ciudad y la abogacía en su ejercicio profesional”, han señalado desde el PSOE tras dar la noticia del fallecimiento. Este luctuoso momento le llega a José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero en un punto de tensión máximo puesto que además está metido de lleno por estar investigado por posibles delitos de tráfico de influencias o blanqueo de capitales.

articles.title: Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears
articles.summary: US president has not endorsed Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 election amid shifting public sentiment.
articles.body:
Washington, DC, United States – Since first entering the White House in 2017, US President Donald Trump has delivered on a right-wing Israeli wish list and pursued a foreign policy that has helped buoy Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political fortunes.

The Israeli leader has, in turn, portrayed himself as the best steward of Israel’s most significant foreign relationship, weathering a handful of public criticisms and leaked discontents from Trump that have yielded little concrete policy change.

But despite the pair’s long history, Trump has so far taken a decidedly ho-hum approach to the October 27 Israeli election . The vote sees Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads under increasing threat from Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and an opposition bloc he seeks to build.

It is an – at least public – ambivalence likely fuelled by shifting political winds in both the US and Israel, as well as the evolving relationship between Trump and Netanyahu, according to Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington DC.

“He seems to be keeping greater distance from it than you would think,” Munayyer told Al Jazeera, “given Trump’s past endorsements of right-wing allies, given the history of the Trump-Netanyahu relationship, and just how close Trump and Netanyahu have been”.

The US president thrice dodged a direct endorsement of Netanyahu in a recent Time magazine interview, even as he defended the Israeli prime minister’s leadership ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel.

On Eisenkot, he conceded, “I don’t hear bad things.”

To be sure, Trump’s actions towards Israel – and Netanyahu in particular – have often spoken far louder than his words.

During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump moved the US embassy to Jerusalem, recognised Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights, withdrew from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and spearheaded a series of normalisation agreements with Arab countries that sought to circumvent the Israel-Palestine issue.

During his second term that started in January 2025, he continued to surge even the most destructive US weapons to Israel amid its genocide in Gaza, escalated a crackdown on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and, as a crown jewel, entered a global economy-rattling war with Iran .

Trump has also called for Netanyahu to be pardoned in his ongoing corruption trial, while hosting the Israeli leader at least seven times since returning to the White House last year, far more than any other world leader.

Throughout their relationship, hints of discord over Netanyahu’s obstruction of Washington’s push for a more lasting peace in Gaza and an end to the war with Iran have never materialised into actual policy changes.

“It’s a relationship they’ve carefully choreographed for public consumption, and the few juicy bits that we’ve learned have been almost entirely of Trump’s choosing,” said Michael Omer-Man, Israel-Palestine director at the Washington, DC-based DAWN think tank, who did not rule out a sweeping US gesture to boost Netanyahu in the final stretch of the race.

“I don’t think that Trump’s abandoned Netanyahu,” he told Al Jazeera. “But he’s also a realist, and he’s seen a lot of his preferred candidates in various countries lose elections as well as win them.”

The stakes may just not be that high for Trump, Omer-Man assessed.

Eisenkot has promised a more moderate approach than Netanyahu’s, particularly when it comes to stemming rampant settler violence in the occupied West Bank. But those changes are largely aimed at boosting Israel’s standing among European governments and the global public, with little bearing on already permissive relations with the Trump administration.

“I don’t think we would see a whole lot of change vis-a-vis the US, because there doesn’t seem to be a whole lot of friction in the relationship,” he said.

“An Eisenkot government might stop taking over every single hilltop in the West Bank; they might allow more [aid] into Gaza,” he said, “but they’re not going to reverse any of the steps that have already been taken.”

Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel at the International Crisis Group, also pointed to the shifting context surrounding Trump and Netanyahu’s relationship.

Trump’s reticence reflects, in part, a divide within the Trump administration over Netanyahu’s government, which reflects a wider Republican Party divide as US midterm elections approach.

“It’s probably a combination of the Iran war and the split in the Trump administration with people like [Vice President JD] Vance, who have come out very much against Netanyahu’s role in pushing for the US to strike Iran,” said Zonszein.

Public opinion polls have repeatedly suggested support for Israel remains high among Republicans, but has ticked down in recent years. Confidence in Netanyahu has also declined within the party.

At the same time, the perception of Trump’s influence has shifted in Israel, with Netanyahu’s critics seizing on the US role in constraining Israeli operations in Lebanon that threatened to derail a June memorandum of understanding that briefly paused the US-Israel war on Iran.

An Israeli Democracy Institute poll released in June found only 44 percent of Jewish Israelis thought Israel’s security was a top consideration for Trump, down from 61 percent in March, shortly after the US and Israel launched the war with Iran.

For his part, Netanyahu has avoided the billboards boasting his close relationship with Trump this election cycle, a departure from his approach in years past, Zonszein explained.

Instead, he has featured who he considers to be Israel’s top regional and international foes, including Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Netanyahu, Zonszein said, is highlighting “his enemies versus his friends”.

articles.title: Trump donor says he’ll sue Guilfoyle, attorneys
articles.summary: The MAGA donor who accused U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle of pressuring him to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express bill said he will be taking legal action against her. “I’m going to be suing those lawyers, that law firm, and Kimberly Guilfoyle,” Eric Deters said in an interview with CNN’s…
articles.body:
The MAGA donor who accused U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle of pressuring him to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express bill said he will be taking legal action against her.

“I’m going to be suing those lawyers, that law firm, and Kimberly Guilfoyle,” Eric Deters said in an interview with CNN’s “Anderson Cooper 360” on Monday. “It’s going to be fun.”

Deters accused Guilfoyle’s legal team of making false claims about him following The Wall Street Journal’s explosive report exposing her pricey request. Guilfoyle allegedly offered to help him reach senior Trump administration officials in exchange.

“They first said that the text messages were fake — defamation,” he said. “Then they said I was a known blackmailer. I’ve never blackmailed anybody in my life.”

Guilfoyle — the ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and the former fiancee of President Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. — and her attorneys have since denied that claim, maintaining that she was seeking to collect roughly $150,000 in unpaid fees for speaking engagements and consulting work.

Deters, a longtime supporter of Trump, told the Journal that he paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over several years to speak at Freedom Fest, a conservative Kentucky-based event he launched in 2020 in opposition to COVID-19 mandates. He also described their relationship as a “quid pro quo.”

The donor shot down that explanation Monday, saying the diplomat never mentioned an outstanding debt in their private messages .

“Now, they’re claiming that there are invoices when she knows that’s not true. In all the text messages, she doesn’t mention anything about me owing money,” he said. “She knows that is phony, and I’m going to be suing them all for defamation.”

In a separate report, the Journal alleged Guilfoyle bragged about her connections to wealthy Greek men who were bankrolling her luxury travel, and that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are weighing whether to fire her.

Trump confirmed Monday that he was aware of the allegations and that her future in the administration was under review.

“Well, we’re looking at it. Yeah, we’re not happy,” the president told The Hill when speaking with reporters on the White House South Lawn.

The Journal also reported that the State Department’s inspector general is investigating her alleged misconduct, and whether the ambassador leveraged her diplomatic position and connections in exchange for gifts or favors from private businessmen.

Deters said he believes Trump should fire her for her actions.

“I think she’s gone. I think he has to fire her,” he told CNN. “It’s grifting on the highest level, and it’s just an awful look for the administration.”

articles.title: Just 1 in 4 approve of Trump handling of economy: Survey
articles.summary: Roughly one-fourth of respondents to a recent survey approve of President Trump’s handling of the economy, with midterm early voting already underway in some states. Just 28 percent of 2,275 respondents to the Financial Times/Focaldata poll approved of Trump’s handling of jobs and the economy. The president’s overall approval rating was 34 percent, with 59…
articles.body:
Roughly one-fourth of respondents to a recent survey approve of President Trump’s handling of the economy, with midterm early voting already underway in some states.

Just 28 percent of 2,275 respondents to the Financial Times/Focaldata poll approved of Trump’s handling of jobs and the economy. The president’s overall approval rating was 34 percent, with 59 percent of respondents disapproving of his performance.

Trump campaigned on lowering prices before voters elected him to the presidency a second time, but inflation has worsened slightly during his time in office.

Annual inflation, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI), has increased from 3 percent in January 2025 to 3.4 percent in August . The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) will release CPI data for September on Wednesday.

Inflation was down to 2.4 percent in February, but the Iran war has resulted in oil price spikes that have translated to higher energy costs stateside. Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.34 per gallon as of Tuesday, $1.26 higher than a year ago, according to data from AAA .

Just 2 in 10 respondents to the Financial Times/Focaldata survey approved of Trump’s handling of inflation, tied with housing for the category where he had the lowest marks.

The survey, which Focaldata conducted from Oct. 2-4, has a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.

Price pressures are not solely concentrated in the energy sector. Beth Hammack, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, noted Monday that the president’s tariffs and rising demand for artificial intelligence are raising prices.

“Energy has been making headlines this year, with prices rising for oil, retail gasoline, and diesel, but it isn’t the whole story,” Hammack said at the annual meeting of the National Association of Business Economics.

Persistent inflation drove the Fed to raise interest rates by a quarter point last month, with the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee set to meet again in two weeks.

The U.S. economy also added 29,000 jobs in September, as the unemployment rate ticked up slightly to 4.2 percent, according to the BLS. Unemployment has remained within a range of 3.4 percent to 4.5 percent since October 2021.

Trump’s approval rating being underwater has coincided with Democrats having increasing odds of taking back control of both chambers of Congress next month. Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s partner, gives Democrats a 54 percent chance to win the Senate and House.

Ahead of the midterms, the president has taken to the campaign trail in a bid to boost turnout. During a Monday rally in Ohio , he again vowed to send $5,000 dividend checks to Americans if Republicans maintain their grip on Congress.

“If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country, the likes of which we have never seen before,” Trump remarked.

articles.title: Omar fundraising off federal investigation
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) released a fundraising email focused on the federal investigation for which agents raided her home on Monday. “Stand with Ilhan Omar,” the email reads, according to a screenshot obtained by The Hill’s partner network, NewsNation. “Donald Trump and DHS have opened a baseless, partisan investigation into Ilhan Omar, and she needs…
articles.body:
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) released a fundraising email focused on the federal investigation for which agents raided her home on Monday.

“Stand with Ilhan Omar,” the email reads, according to a screenshot obtained by The Hill’s partner network, NewsNation. “Donald Trump and DHS have opened a baseless, partisan investigation into Ilhan Omar, and she needs us by her side as they escalate their attacks.”

“Chip in whatever you can to make sure Ilhan can beat Trump and keep fighting for our progressive values in Congress,” the email concludes.

On Monday morning, Homeland Security Investigations — the investigative arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — searched Omar’s home as part of an ongoing criminal investigation into the Minnesota Democrat, according to a statement from the Department of Justice (DOJ).

White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed in September that Omar was under criminal investigation but did not give further details about it.

“I’m confirming that ICE is, yeah — look, I said months ago that there’s something that’s been reported and needs to be looked at,” Homan said.

It is unusual for the DOJ to take major action against candidates for office within 60 days of an election, and the midterms are only three weeks away.

Omar condemned the raid in a post online, calling it “political intimidation.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on the social platform X . “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

Omar has repeatedly clashed with President Trump during her tenure in the House, criticizing the president’s comments about Somali immigrants and his accusation that refugees from the African nation are “completely taking over the once great state of Minnesota.”

The president also lashed out at Omar at a gaggle with reporters before he rallied in Ohio, calling her “totally crooked” and a “terrible person.” At a Cabinet meeting earlier this year Trump also called her “garbage” while saying he did not want Somali people in the U.S., and at one point he said Somalia “stinks.”

articles.title: Boebert: Iran war ‘detrimental on many levels’
articles.summary: Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) spoke out against the Iran war when pressed during a Monday debate about whether the military conflict was worth its cost to the American public. “I never wanted us to be at war in Iran,” Boebert said. “This has been detrimental on many levels. “I also will stand by and say…
articles.body:
Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) spoke out against the Iran war when pressed during a Monday debate about whether the military conflict was worth its cost to the American public.

“I never wanted us to be at war in Iran,” Boebert said. “This has been detrimental on many levels.

“I also will stand by and say that President Trump is the commander-in-chief, and he is not the first president to use force through his powers as commander-in-chief,” she continued. “I do agree that this is expensive, and I hear from Republicans, unaffiliated and Democrats that they want this to come to an end, and so do I.”

The Republican Party has faced an uphill battle headed into the midterm elections amid rising public discontent with the Middle East conflict and the strain it has placed on global energy markets.

The average cost of standard gasoline in the U.S. was up to around $4.34 per gallon on Tuesday — over a 40 percent increase from a year ago, according to AAA . In a CNN and SSRS poll conducted last month, 64 percent of Americans polled said the U.S. was not winning with the military operation against Tehran, which has now stretched over seven months.

9News moderator Kyle Clark asked Boebert about what Congress was doing to try to bring the war to a close.

“We are having conversations with the Department of War and with the president and his administration on a regular basis about how to come to an end with this,” the Colorado Republican replied.

“A symbolic, procedural vote put on by progressive Democrats is not going to be the answer and to give Iran a clear end date so then they can do something afterwards,” she added.

Her Democratic challenger, retired Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, slammed the GOP incumbent over her refusal to back war powers resolutions in the House to urge the Trump administration to bring the conflict to a close.

“Your job is to vote whether or not you think the war should continue, and Ms. Boebert has voted now I believe five times to keep this war going,” Laubacher said.

“And so, you can say all day long that you don’t want there to be war and you want it to draw to a close, but you’re not using your voice to raise the voices of the people you describe in Congressional District 4 who are opposed to this war,” the Democratic nominee continued.

“Your job is to be their voice in Congress, their voice to the president, saying we do not want this war, and you are failing to do that,” she added.

Boebert is running for reelection in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, which has been reliably red for over a decade. The district includes a large farming and ranching community, a population that has become increasingly skeptical of the Trump administration’s tariffs.
