articles.title: Don’t let America’s enemies use defamation lawsuits as proxy warfare
articles.summary: A lawsuit brought by Azerbaijan against CNN offers an early glimpse of what full-blown sovereign international lawfare in American courts could look like.
articles.body:
Expectations for the September summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Trump were low and were largely met. The meeting produced a few modest agreements , including additional economic talks and new channels for discussing artificial intelligence and preventing military crises , but the fundamental disputes between Washington and Beijing remain unresolved.

This is no surprise. A stalemate was widely predicted, and few incentives exist for compromise right now. This doesn’t mean the competition will stop. Instead, it will migrate. Domestic stalemates tend to empower the courts. International stalemates increasingly do the same.

International lawfare is nothing new, and China has become particularly adept at using legal mechanisms as an instrument of statecraft. As Washington and Beijing settle into prolonged strategic competition, American courts will inevitably become another arena where both sides seek leverage.

Chinese entities are already testing the limits of American jurisprudence. Chinese automaker BYD sued both the Alliance for American Manufacturing and VICE Media for defamation. More recently, Chinese semiconductor company Yangtze Memory Technologies sued the Danish firm Strand Consult over allegedly false and damaging statements. Each case stemmed from allegations that the companies were cooperating with the Chinese government. Courts dismissed all three cases.

Now, a lawsuit brought by Azerbaijan against CNN offers an early glimpse of what full-blown sovereign international lawfare in American courts could look like.

Azerbaijan has sued CNN in federal court over a June report alleging that Israel had used Azerbaijani territory for military and intelligence operations against Iran. Azerbaijan says the allegations were false, relied on anonymous sources and ignored the government’s denials before publication. Azerbaijan argues that CNN’s reporting created a national security threat, exposing the country and its citizens to retaliation. Iran had already attacked Azerbaijan in March. CNN has stood by its reporting.

Azerbaijan is asking an American court to consider whether a sovereign entity can seek damages when false reporting produces concrete security consequences. The complaint acknowledges this as a novel legal question — a test case. American courts have historically been deeply skeptical of U.S. state and federal government agencies and offices using defamation law against their domestic critics, particularly the press.

Whether the U.S. legal system distinguishes between criticism of a government by its own citizens and allegations about a foreign sovereign state made by an American media organization remains an open question. Azerbaijan’s argument invites courts to distinguish between domestic and foreign government plaintiffs.

Azerbaijan may have a legitimate grievance. However, if American courts recognize a foreign sovereign’s ability to bring such claims against the U.S. press, they will create a mechanism available not only to Azerbaijan. A precedent permitting a foreign government to sue American media organizations over alleged national security damage could easily be invoked by Beijing, Chinese state-owned enterprises or other state-linked entities.

China itself could argue that false reporting about its activities caused measurable economic or national security harm. Beijing could then seek to turn what was previously a political dispute into a legal proceeding. The lawsuit would not have to succeed to cause damage.

The United States has spent years building its China policy around executive orders. Congress has often responded after the fact, leaving the courts to interpret an increasingly complicated collection of rules and rulings. This is a vulnerability. Sustained competition with China requires durable statutory authorities, clear congressional mandates and predictable judicial standards. Otherwise, every new restriction invites litigation, and every legal ambiguity becomes another potential avenue for Chinese leverage.

The answer is not to prevent foreign actors from using American courts or to dismiss Azerbaijan’s lawsuit against CNN because of what Beijing might do. Nor should Washington weaken judicial independence simply because China might eventually exploit a precedent. Those principles are precisely what make the American system durable.

Instead, Congress has a few actionable bipartisan bills it can advance to preempt Chinese lawfare. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

Congress can strengthen safeguards for journalists reporting on foreign activities through the Granite Act and establish a definition of transnational repression that includes lawfare through amendments to the STOP TNR Act . The SAMS Act of 2025 can codify ever-contentious critical minerals executive orders, while the Restoring American Mineral Security Act empowers trade representatives to work with foreign partners to counter Chinese critical minerals initiatives.

Meanwhile, the COINS Act of 2025 , enacted through the 2026 defense authorization, directs the Treasury Department to restrict certain U.S. investments in countries of concern involving sensitive technologies. These are all steps in the right direction.

These stalled bills, among many worthy considerations backlogged by congressional myopia, must be passed. Pleading for bipartisan action on common-sense bills is a thoroughly American tradition I must now indulge. Many more worthy bills remain unlisted here, and reasonable minds will disagree on which ones to prioritize. But at least some of them must be advanced to preempt a predictable deluge of lawfare.

If Washington fails to grasp the urgency, Beijing will not fail to seize the opportunity.

Wesley Alexander Hill is the associate director and lead analyst for the Energy, Growth, and Security Program at the International Tax and Investment Center. Hill focuses mostly on Chinese influence in the Global South and Sino-American energy competition.

articles.title: Sherrod Brown says he would not support impeaching Trump if elected
articles.summary: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is fighting a tough race to win his way back to the Senate, says he will not support impeaching President Trump again if Democrats win control of Congress in next month’s election. Brown voted twice to convict Trump on impeachment charges in 2020 and 2021 before losing reelection in…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is fighting a tough race to win his way back to the Senate, says he will not support impeaching President Trump again if Democrats win control of Congress in next month’s election.

Brown voted twice to convict Trump on impeachment charges in 2020 and 2021 before losing reelection in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Now, he wants Democrats to skip another impeachment battle if they win back the House and possibly the Senate, too, on Nov. 3.

“I can’t speak for everybody else, but I would not support an impeachment of Trump,” Brown told The Columbus Dispatch. “There’s simply no reason for that, no matter what happens in the midterms.”

Brown is in a neck-and-neck race with Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in a state that Trump carried with 55 percent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election. Thep resident handily defeated Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 11-percentage points.

Husted has sought to rev up the Republican vote by campaigning with Trump.

The duo appeared at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Monday evening, where the president touted the incumbent senator as “a great athlete,” referring to his time as an All-American defensive back for the Division III Dayton Flyers.

Republicans are bracing for another Democratic effort to impeach Trump if Democrats capture the House, as political handicappers and Decision Desk HQ now project.

Several House Democrats have already introduced articles of impeachment against Trump in the current Congress and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to become the next Speaker, isn’t ruling out another push.

“No, we haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” Jeffries told George Stephanopoulos on ABC’s “This Week” in September.

House Democrats impeached Trump twice when they controlled the majority in 2019 and 2021.

The first impeachment effort sought to remove him from office on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, alleging that the president unlawfully pressed Ukrainian officials to influence the 2020 presidential election.

House Democrats and a handful of Republicans voted to impeach Trump a second time on Jan. 13, 2021, accusing him of inciting insurrection after a mob of his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, in a failed attempt to stop the certification of the 2020 presidential election.

Trump was acquitted both times in the Senate, where Democrats would have needed 67 votes or a two-thirds majority to convict him and remove him from office or bar him from running for office again.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told conservative pundit Scott Jennings in a recent interview that Democrats would move immediately to impeach Trump a third time if they win control of the House.

“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day – first or second day,” Johnson predicted. “Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress. And they’re raring to go.”

articles.title: Sotomayor, Gorsuch condemn immigrant’s prosecution, citing ‘constitutional absurdity’
articles.summary: A liberal and conservative Supreme Court justice joined forces on Tuesday to condemn what they said were “serious constitutional problems” in the government’s prosecution of a Mexican national for illegally reentering the country. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, said it was difficult to see how Jesus Herrera-Salazar’s treatment squared with double jeopardy protections. “Should…
articles.body:
A liberal and conservative Supreme Court justice joined forces on Tuesday to condemn what they said were “serious constitutional problems” in the government’s prosecution of a Mexican national for illegally reentering the country.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, said it was difficult to see how Jesus Herrera-Salazar’s treatment squared with double jeopardy protections.

“Should circumstances like these arise again, I encourage courts to avoid the constitutional absurdity that occurred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning,” Sotomayor wrote.

The Supreme Court turns away the vast majority of requests to take up cases, and it did so with Herrera-Salazar’s on Tuesday alongside dozens of other appeals.

Sotomayor and Gorsuch agreed with their colleagues they shouldn’t have taken up the case, noting that Herrera-Salazar was already deported. But the duo cautioned they hoped the facts of his case “are anomalous.”

The government prosecuted Herrera-Salazar twice after saying he illegally crossed the border on “numerous occasions.”

First, he was found in Texas in 2020 and sentenced to prison time. Afterward — while still on supervised release and required to remain on U.S. soil under law enforcement’s watch — he was found in Oklahoma. He was convicted of illegal reentry once again.

Herrera-Salazar has served both sentences and was removed from the country in 2024, court documents indicate.

But he had continued to argue the subsequent round violated the Fifth Amendment’s protections against prosecutions “for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.”

The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found no violation, saying each of his convictions were for separate offenses.

It’s not the first time that Sotomayor, an appointee of former President Obama, and Gorsuch, President Trump’s first Supreme Court appointee, have teamed up to speak out publicly about a criminal defendant’s treatment.

“When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves continuous, uninterrupted conduct, our precedents and the logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that the Government is barred from charging that defendant with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by focusing on a different time marker,” Sotomayor wrote, joined by Gorsuch.

articles.body:
Anthony Scaramucci is weighing in on Katie Zacharia’s first briefing as White House press secretary, quipping that the clock is ticking on her tenure.

“The clock is running,” Scaramucci wrote on X on Tuesday, shortly after Zacharia wrapped her inaugural briefing at the White House as press secretary.

“Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci,” he cracked.

Scaramucci famously served a speedy stint — just 10 days — as White House communications director in 2017 during President Trump’s first term in office.

The hedge fund founder’s remarks came after Zacharia held what Trump had described as an “introductory news conference” in the press briefing room on Tuesday after being named the new White House press secretary last week.

Zacharia stepped into the role following the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration earlier this year.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Trump Media communications adviser, took questions from three members of the press during the 14-minute briefing.

articles.title: Trump: Marshall was ‘mandated by law’ to request payments from patients
articles.summary: President Trump defended Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) after a report revealed that he sued hundreds of patients for unpaid medical bills, claiming the senator was legally obligated to pursue the debts or risk facing criminal charges himself. In a lengthy Truth Social post on Monday, Trump praised the former obstetrician-gynecologist and accused his Democratic challenger,…
articles.body:
President Trump defended Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) after a report revealed that he sued hundreds of patients for unpaid medical bills, claiming the senator was legally obligated to pursue the debts or risk facing criminal charges himself.

In a lengthy Truth Social post on Monday, Trump praised the former obstetrician-gynecologist and accused his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton, of using the controversy against him ahead of November’s election.

“Roger is one of my favorite Senators — He is absolutely GREAT, a wonderful person, given a ‘bum rap’ because he was mandated by Law to request money owed from patients,” Trump wrote. “If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the Law, and subject to criminal liability and arrest.”

There is no federal or state law requiring doctors to sue patients over unpaid medical bills, nor is there such a law requiring debt collectors to request arrest warrants from judges for defendants who do not show up to court.

A September investigation by The New York Times revealed that Marshall’s medical practice sued more than 700 patients over outstanding bills during his decades-long career as a physician, including some debts as low as $101.

Patients were arrested in 81 of those cases after missing court appearances, according to the records reviewed by the Times. Marshall’s attorneys sought arrest warrants in 13 cases, though it was unclear whether those patients were taken into custody.

Trump also defended Marshall over the arrests, arguing that judges, rather than the senator, were responsible for enforcing court orders.

“A judge ordering a patient’s arrest for not showing up to court many, many times is not Roger Marshall’s fault — IT IS THE LAW,” he wrote.

Kansas law allows judges to issue arrest warrants when defendants fail to appear in court, but attorneys are not required to request them. The Times found that Marshall’s lawyers repeatedly sought warrants against patients who missed court dates.

Steve Johnson, an attorney for Marshall who regularly represented the senator in debt cases, said in a statement to the Times that the warrants were necessary to ensure the debtors were present in court.

“If defendants were allowed to appear only when they wanted to without any consequences the court would get no business done,” he said.

Johnson also told the outlet that Marshall was not personally involved in decisions to seek arrest warrants or garnish patients’ wages. He did, however, say Marshall established an 18 percent annual interest rate on outstanding medical bills.

articles.body:
In her second day on the job, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters that the White House has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, following multiple reports that created a scandal surrounding her post.

President Trump, on departing the White House for Alaska, said about Guilfoyle, “I didn’t like what I read.”

In a post on her personal X account following the briefing, Guilfoyle denied the reported allegations: “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

A lawyer and former conservative commentator, Zacharia held her first briefing after joining the administration late last week.

President Trump on Tuesday is heading to Alaska , his sixth trip there since 2019, to rally support for incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). His main opponent, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D), has been leading him in the polls for much of the fall, according to the Decision Desk HQ polling average . Trump will speaks from Wasilla at 7:30 p.m. EDT.

Vice President Vance will visit Tyler, Texas, on Tuesday at midday to stump for Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), who is running for his third term in the Lone Star State’s 1st Congressional District.

Several marquee midterm races will hold debates on Tuesday night: Florida and Maine Senate races at 7 p.m. EDT; Georgia Senate at 8 p.m. EDT; Iowa Senate at 10 p.m. EDT, along with gubernatorial debates in Maine, New York, Illinois and Oregon, and another forum for the Los Angeles mayoral race.

articles.title: Schumer: Republicans heading into midterms with ‘enormous’ financial advantage
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is warning his Democratic colleagues that Senate Republican candidates have an “enormous” financial advantage heading into the final three weeks before Election Day and could drown Democrats’ chances of winning the Senate in a “tsunami” of last-minute spending. Schumer is warning in a “Dear Colleague” letter circulated Tuesday that…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is warning his Democratic colleagues that Senate Republican candidates have an “enormous” financial advantage heading into the final three weeks before Election Day and could drown Democrats’ chances of winning the Senate in a “tsunami” of last-minute spending.

Schumer is warning in a “Dear Colleague” letter circulated Tuesday that the “battle for control of the Senate ” may depend on whether an “unprecedented tsunami of Republican money” can defeat the advantage Democratic candidates have running in a favorable political climate.

Schumer argues that Democrats are “winning the argument” in key Senate races across the country by emphasizing the issue of affordability and pointing to rising prices and allegations of government corruption under Trump.

But he warned that Democratic message may get completely drowned out by hundreds of millions of dollars that Trump’s super PAC and Elon Musk , the world’s wealthiest man, are pouring into Senate races.

“We have strong candidates, a clear message, and a political climate that offers real opportunities. But Republicans have one enormous advantage of their own. Money,” Schumer wrote to colleagues.

Schumer noted that Trump could spend between $400 million and $500 million from his super PAC, MAGA Inc., to support Republican candidates and that Musk has funneled close to $300 million into the midterm races to help Republicans.

He said that other “megadonors” are also pouring money into Senate races in amounts “unlike we’ve ever seen before.”

“That’s the enormous force bearing down on this election. And it’s a challenge none of us can afford to underestimate,” he wrote.

Republican campaigns, committees and allied groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by about $400 million so far this election cycle, according to data from AdImpact reported by Fox News.

Yet, Democrats had a big spending advantage in the 2024 presidential election, when Vice President Kamala Harris and her Democratic allies spent approximately twice as much as Trump and his allies on political ads.

Despite the Democratic spending advantage, Trump still soundly defeated Harris and Republicans recaptured control of the Senate two years ago.

Schumer told colleagues, however, the good news for Democrats this year is that Trump’s unpopularity and voters’ anger over high costs are weighing on Republican candidates.

He noted that some polls show that only 30 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s job performance and 78 percent of Americans blame Trump for rising costs.

“Over the last two years, our caucus has worked every day to make sure the American people understand that Senate Republicans are responsible for the costs they are paying and the pain they are feeling,” he wrote.

articles.body:
Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) maintained a strong lead in the state’s Senate race in a new poll released Tuesday.

The WRAL/WSOC poll , which was conducted by SurveyUSA, found the Democrat with a 14-point advantage over former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley.

Cooper’s lead exceeded the survey’s margin of error and was his strongest polling result. Fifty-four percent of likely North Carolina voters said they would back the former governor in the November contest, while 40 percent expressed their support for the Republican nominee.

Early voting in North Carolina begins this week.

The two candidates are competing in the open race to replace retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R), who announced his departure from Congress following repeated clashes with President Trump over a massive tax and spending legislative package.

Tillis recently endorsed Whatley in the race to replace him, but he warned the Republican candidate against campaigning with Trump amid the president’s low job approval ratings .

Trump told reporters earlier this month that he was “ worried ” about Whatley’s chances in this election. The president stumped for the Republican nominee in September, following the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.
